title: Breach in the Flat Network
role: You are the network security engineer after a laptop compromise.
objective: Contain the breach and design segmentation so that the next compromise cannot reach the crown jewels.
environment: The internal network is flat: every internal address can reach every other, and the VPN trusts all internal addresses. Finance databases, domain controllers and backups share the network with laptops.

hud.label: Systems reachable from a compromised host

state_variables.blast_radius: Systems reachable from a compromised host, starts at 100

stages.narrative: Logs show an attacker moving from a laptop towards the finance database.
stages.decision_prompt: How do you contain the live incident?

choices.text: Isolate the laptop and its credentials, apply a temporary rule blocking east-west traffic from it, and keep business traffic running.
choices.feedback: Correct. Contain the specific foothold and its paths while the rest of the business continues.
It contains the breach but halts the business, and you lose live visibility of what the attacker is doing.

choices.text: Do nothing until the root cause is known.
choices.feedback: The attacker keeps moving while you investigate. Contain first, then investigate.

stages.narrative: Leadership wants segmentation. You have no map of who talks to whom.

choices.text: Capture flow data for two weeks to see which systems actually communicate, then write allow-lists from the evidence.
choices.feedback: Correct. Policies written from observed flows break less and stay accurate.

choices.text: Draw segments from the org chart and block everything else at once.
choices.feedback: It shrinks the blast radius, but undocumented dependencies fail at once and operations suffer.
The attacker was already inside the perimeter; a stronger edge does not stop lateral movement.

stages.narrative: You have flow data and can segment in phases.

choices.text: The crown jewels: finance databases, domain controllers and backups, with default-deny and monitored allow-lists.
choices.feedback: Correct. Protecting the highest-value targets first removes the most risk per unit of effort.
Physical location rarely matches risk or data flows; it takes long and protects little.

choices.text: Start with the guest Wi-Fi only.
choices.feedback: Guest Wi-Fi is easy and worthwhile, but it was not the attack path and leaves the crown jewels exposed.

stages.narrative: Segments exist. Internal addresses are still implicitly trusted by the VPN and admin tools.
stages.decision_prompt: What do you do about identity?

choices.text: Apply zero-trust controls for admin access: MFA, per-request authorisation, just-in-time admin rights and no shared accounts.
choices.feedback: Correct. A stolen laptop or password should not be enough to reach a crown jewel; each access is authenticated and authorised.

choices.text: Keep trusting every internal address on the VPN.
choices.feedback: Segmentation without identity checks still lets a compromised trusted address through allowed paths.

choices.text: Rename the hosts so they are harder to guess.
choices.feedback: Obscurity does not stop an attacker who can scan the network.

bands.title: Contained and segmented
bands.text: SUCCESS. The breach was contained without an outage, and the crown jewels now sit behind segments and identity-aware access.

bands.title: Improved, not done
bands.text: PARTIAL. The blast radius is smaller, but either it is still large or the programme cost too much disruption or time.

bands.title: Still flat
bands.text: AT RISK. An attacker with one foothold can still reach most systems.

resolution.concept_reveal: Segmentation and zero trust limit lateral movement: contain the foothold, map real flows, protect high-value assets first with default-deny, and authenticate and authorise every access instead of trusting network location (NIST SP 800-207).

replayability_note: Different orders of work lead to different disruption; replay to compare.
